sec.title: Background
sec.p: The differentiation of macrophages into foam cells is a hallmark of atherosclerotic plaques, and macrophage polarization is a key driver of disease progression, yet the underlying genetic mechanisms remain poorly understood. We employed summary data-based Mendelian randomization (SMR) combined with transcriptomic validation to explore causal relationships and validate findings at the tissue level.

sec.title: Methods
sec.p: We integrated multi-omics data, including DNA methylation (mQTLs), gene expression (eQTLs), and protein expression (pQTLs), from GeneCards and GWAS summary statistics from FinnGen and UK Biobank. SMR and colocalization analyses were used to identify causal associations. Tissue-specific validation was conducted using eQTL data from artery tissues, and transcriptome analysis was performed using GEO datasets to confirm gene expression patterns in atherosclerotic tissues, followed by confirmation in clinical samples. The function of key genes were explored using Gene Ontology (GO) and Kyoto Encyclopedia of Genes and Genomes (KEGG) analysis.

sec.title: Results
sec.p: SMR and colocalization analyses identified 41 methylation sites, 2 genes (DNMT3A and DLGAP5), and 1 protein associated with atherosclerosis. Specifically, methylation site cg10130446 in DLGAP5 was negatively correlated with atherosclerosis, while sites cg08485187 and cg17742416 in DNMT3A were positively associated. Tissue-specific validation revealed that SIRT6 gene expression was linked to atherosclerosis risk in aortic and tibial artery tissues. Transcriptome analysis from GEO database and blood samples confirmed elevated DLGAP5 and SIRT6 expressions.

sec.title: Conclusions
sec.p: This study integrates SMR with transcriptomic validation to reveal causal links between macrophage polarization-related genes and atherosclerosis. Key genes DNMT3A, DLGAP5, and SIRT6 were identified as significant candidate regulatory factors. Tissue-specific validation and GEO-based transcriptome analysis provided robust evidence supporting these findings, highlighting the importance of macrophage polarization in atherosclerosis pathogenesis and offering new insights for therapeutic intervention.

sec.title: Background
sec.p: Atherosclerosis (AS) is a chronic inflammatory disease characterized by lipid accumulation in large arteries [1]. As the leading cause of cardiovascular diseases, it accounts for approximately one-third of global deaths, with increasing prevalence worldwide [2–4]. Despite established risk factors such as hyperlipidemia and hypertension [5], the persistent burden of AS underscores the urgent need to elucidate its underlying mechanisms.

Macrophages are crucial immune cells involved in the inflammatory response associated with atherosclerosis [6]. Upon entering the arterial intima, monocytes differentiate into macrophages and can adopt different functional phenotypes based on the local microenvironment. These phenotypes are broadly categorized into M1 and anti-inflammatory (M2) macrophages [6–8]. The balance between M1 and M2 macrophages plays a pivotal role in the progression or regression of atherosclerotic lesions. Advanced single-cell sequencing technologies have revealed the heterogeneity of macrophage populations within atherosclerotic plaques, highlighting the complexity of macrophage polarization and its impact on disease pathology [9]. Macrophage polarization plays an important role in the development of atherosclerosis [10].

Genes involved in macrophage polarization, encompassing those encoding cytokines, transcription factors, and receptors, have been implicated in the modulation of atherosclerotic processes [11]. Notably, key transcriptional regulators such as NF-κB, STAT1, and PPAR-γ play pivotal roles in orchestrating the M1/M2 balance [12]. Previous investigations, ranging from Genome-Wide Association Studies (GWAS) to Mendelian Randomization (MR) analyses, have consistently detected associations between these inflammatory mediators and atherosclerosis [13, 14]. However, a critical limitation in current literature is the conflation of general inflammatory signaling with the specific genetic drivers of macrophage polarization. For instance, while loci such as NFKB1 or PPARG are robustly linked to atherosclerosis, their extensive involvement in broad systemic immune responses makes it difficult to pinpoint whether their pathogenicity stems specifically from the modulation of macrophage polarization mechanisms or merely from generalized systemic inflammation [15, 16]. Consequently, the precise causal architecture—specifically, whether genetic variations within the polarization machinery directly drive atherogenesis independent of systemic inflammatory burdens—remains incompletely elucidated.

Mendelian randomization (MR) is an innovative analytical approach that leverages genetic variants as instrumental variables to infer causal relationships between exposures and outcomes. Unlike observational studies, MR is robust to reverse causation and minimizes confounding, thereby significantly enhancing the accuracy and reliability of its findings [17]. Building on this foundation, summary data-based Mendelian randomization (SMR) has emerged as a powerful extension of MR. SMR enables researchers to explore genetic associations between various molecular traits—such as gene expression, DNA methylation, or protein levels—and diseases of interest using large-scale genomic datasets [18]. By utilizing top cis-quantitative trait loci (cis-QTLs) as exposure variables, SMR achieves greater statistical power, especially when analyses are conducted with independent samples of substantial size. Prior research has demonstrated the efficacy of SMR in identifying and validating pathogenic genes linked to atherosclerosis [19]. Therefore, this approach provides a comprehensive perspective of causal inference between targeted genes and the disease.

Given the crucial role of macrophage polarization in atherosclerosis, this study aimed to identify potential macrophage polarization-related genes in the disease using SMR methods. Using comprehensive multi-omics analysis, this study aims to reveal the complex genetic factors behind atherosclerosis and macrophage polarization. We expect that these findings will not only increase the understanding of the mechanism of the disease, but also provide important theoretical guidance for the development of precision treatment programs and personalized medical pathways.

sec.title: Study design
sec.p: The present investigation employed a comprehensive, stepwise approach to elucidate the role of macrophage polarization-related genes in atherosclerosis susceptibility. As depicted in Fig. 1, our study began by identifying a total of 731 protein-coding genes related to macrophage polarization through the GeneCards database. To strengthen the credibility of our findings, we incorporated instrumental variables selection, utilizing data from three large-scale studies for mQTL, eQTL, and pQTL instruments. Subsequently, we leveraged GWAS data from two independent cohorts - the discovery set from the FinnGen database, and the replication set from the UK Biobank (UKB), followed by SMR and colocalization analysis to confirm the causal relationships between the identified genes and atherosclerosis. After identifying the candidate genes with causal associations, we further performed tissue-specific validation to explore the causal relationship between identified gene expression in tissues and atherosclerosis. Finally, transcriptome analysis was performed using data from the Gene Expression Omnibus (GEO) database to validate the expression of candidate genes in atherosclerotic tissues. The function of these genes were investigated with enrichment analysis and gene-gene network was generated to illustrate their functional associations. Finally, the expression of the key genes identified in this study were confirmed in clinical samples. These methods enabled us to integrate evidence from various omics levels, thereby providing a more comprehensive understanding of the macrophage polarization-related genes and their impact on atherosclerosis susceptibility. All summary statistics utilized for SMR analyses were extracted from previously published studies that already had undergone appropriate ethical approval processes.

sec.title: Sample collection
sec.p: Sample collection was approved by the Ethics Committee of the First Hospital of Jilin University (Approval No.: 2025 − 168), and all participants provided written informed consent. Participants included 6 patients with atherosclerosis (mean age: 67.8 ± 8.2 years; 5 males) confirmed by clinical and imaging methods, and 6 age- and sex-matched healthy subjects (mean age: 68.0 ± 9.0 years; 5 males). Detailed baseline characteristics of the study population are presented in Table 1. Individuals with severe liver or kidney dysfunction, acute infection, malignancy, and autoimmune diseases were excluded. Blood samples (3 mL) were collected from the antecubital vein of all participants in the fasting state in the morning.

sec.title: Data sources
sec.p: Using the keyword “Macrophage Polarization” in the GeneCards database (https://www.genecards.org/), 731 protein-coding genes related to macrophage polarization were retrieved and downloaded.

The discovery cohort utilized the atherosclerosis GWAS data from the FinnGen study (GWAS ID: FinnGen_R10_I9_ATHSCLE) [20], which consists 16,243 cases and 381,977 controls.The phenotype I9_ATHSCLE is defined as atherosclerosis of the arteries, explicitly excluding cerebral and coronary sclerosis to focus on peripheral and generalized arterial pathology (ICD-10 code I70). In contrast, the replication cohort data come from the UK Biobank (GWAS ID: UKB_X440 cohort) [21], which consists 1,324 cases and 400,595 controls, representing generalized atherosclerosis (PheCode 440). Detailed cohort information, including GWAS IDs, sample sizes, and SNP counts, is summarized in Supplementary Table S1. Blood eQTL data for macrophage polarization genes were obtained from eQTLGen, including genetic data on blood gene expression from 31,684 individuals [22]. Blood mQTL summary data were obtained from the Brisbane Systems Genetics Study (n = 614) and the Lothian Birth Cohorts (n = 1366) [23]. Blood pQTL summary data were obtained from Sun et al., including 54,219 UKB participants [24].

Subsequently, tissue-specific expression eQTL data from the GTEx database (https://gtexportal.org/home/) were used to assess the tissue-specific expression of target genes and explore their potential causal impact on atherosclerosis. The GTEx v8 dataset includes 838 donors and 17,382 samples from 52 tissues and two cell lines. For the analysis of atherosclerosis, eQTL data from Artery_Aorta, Artery_Coronary, and Artery_Tibial were used.

For GEO validation, the microarray dataset GSE100927 was retrieved from the GEO database, comprising 104 samples: 69 atherosclerotic tissues from the carotid, femoral, and infra-popliteal arteries, and 35 non-atherosclerotic tissues.

sec.title: Summary-data-based MR analysis
sec.p: The SMR and HEIDI tests were implemented using the SMR software tool (SMR v1.3.1). SMR was used to evaluate the relationships between methylation, expression, and protein abundance of macrophage polarization genes and atherosclerosis. When the exposure and outcome come from two large independent cohorts, SMR, based on the top associated cis-QTL, provides higher statistical power than traditional MR analysis [25]. In this study, we selected the top cis-QTLs within a ± 1000 kb window around the corresponding gene, applying a P-value threshold of 5.0 × 10⁻⁸ [26]. To ensure the quality and consistency of our dataset, single nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs) showing allele frequency discrepancies exceeding a threshold of 0.2 across any paired datasets (including LD reference samples, QTL summary statistics, and outcome summary statistics) were excluded from the analysis. The maximum allowable proportion of SNPs with allele frequency differences was set to the default value of 0.05 (corresponding to the parameter --diff-freq-prop 0.05).

In this study, we extended our investigation into the causal relationships between quantitative trait loci (QTLs)—specifically, methylation QTLs (mQTL), expression QTLs (eQTL), and protein QTLs (pQTL)—and atherosclerosis. We also explored the potential causal associations between mQTL and eQTL by framing mQTL as the exposure variable and eQTL as the outcome variable. To enhance the analysis, we developed an advanced multi-SNP-based summary data-based Mendelian randomization (SMR) method (--smr-multi), which incorporates multiple single nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs) within QTL regions [27]. This method integrates all SNPs in a window centered on the QTL ± 500 kb in SMR analysis, whose p value is less than the default value 5.0 × 10− 8, and the LD r2 value of top-related SNPs is less than the default value 0.9. To distinguish between pleiotropic effects and linkage, we applied the heterogeneity in dependent instruments (HEIDI) test. A P-HEIDI value greater than 0.05 indicates that the observed associations are unlikely due to pleiotropy. By setting thresholds of P_SMR_multi < 0.05, P_SMR < 0.05, and P-HEIDI > 0.05, we identified results that met these criteria for further colocalization analyses among mQTL, eQTL, and pQTL, as well as for integration analysis.

Our analytic framework was rigorously designed to satisfy the three core assumptions of Mendelian randomization: relevance, independence, and exclusion restriction. The relevance assumption was ensured by selecting top cis-QTLs with genome-wide significance (P < 5.0 × 10− 8) as instrumental variables, guaranteeing a strong association with the exposure. To address the independence and exclusion restriction assumptions, we applied the HEIDI test to distinguish true causality from linkage disequilibrium (LD) or horizontal pleiotropy. A P-HEIDI > 0.05 was strictly used as the criterion to filter out pleiotropic signals, thereby supporting the inference that the genetic instruments affect atherosclerosis risk solely through the target molecular traits.

sec.title: Colocalization analysis
sec.p: Colocalization analysis was conducted using the ‘coloc’ R package to identify shared causal variants between AR and macrophage polarization-related mQTLs, eQTLs and pQTLs. Five mutually exclusive hypotheses were tested: (1) H0: No association with SNPs in the region for either trait; (2) H1: Association with SNPs in the region for trait 1 only; (3) H2: Association with SNPs in the region for trait 2 only; (4) H3: Association with SNPs in the region for both traits, but with different causal variants; (5) H4: Association with SNPs in the region for both traits, sharing the same causal variant. Robust evidence of colocalization was established when the posterior probability for H4 (PPH4) was greater than 0.5, assuming p12 was set to 5 × 10− 5, with the co-localization region windows delineated as ± 1000 kb [28].

Colocalization analysis was performed on SNPs in the top cis-QTL colocalization region windows ± 1000 kb. Parameters were set according to Pairo-Castineira et al., with the colocalization threshold defined as P12 = 5 × 10− 5 and PPH4 > 0.5 as the posterior probability for colocalization [28].

sec.title: Multi-omics integration and gene prioritization strategy
sec.p: To systematically identify key genes, we employed a hierarchical prioritization strategy. First, genes were screened for significant causal associations (P_SMR < 0.05) in at least one omics level (mQTL, eQTL, or pQTL), with pleiotropy excluded by the HEIDI test (P_HEIDI > 0.05). Second, we prioritized candidates showing consistent evidence across multiple omics layers, specifically focusing on the intersection of mQTL, eQTL, and pQTL hits. Finally, these candidates were rigorously validated using tissue-specific eQTL data and clinical differential expression analysis to confirm their biological relevance.

sec.title: Differential genes expression
sec.p: To retrieve the genes differentially expressed between atherosclerotic and normal tissues, we employed the “limma” package on the microarray dataset GSE100927 from the GEO database, which contained atherosclerotic lesions and control arteries without atherosclerotic lesions. Differentially expressed genes were filtered via the Wilcoxon test under the threshold (|logFC| > 0 & P.Value < 0.05). The R packages “FactoMineR” and “factoextra” were used for principal component analysis (PCA) and its visualization. Heatmaps were visualized using the “pheatmap” package.

sec.title: Enrichment analysis
sec.p: To elucidate the function of DLGAP5 and SIRT6, we conducted Gene Ontology (GO) enrichment and Kyoto Encyclopedia of Genes and Genomes (KEGG) analysis to explore the biological processes (BP), molecular functions (MF), and cellular components (CC) of these genes. The package “Clusterprofiler” was used for GO and KEGG analysis and visualization. P values were adjusted using the Benjamini-Hochberg method.

sec.title: Gene-gene interaction network
sec.p: To elucidate the functional associations of DLGAP5 and SIRT6, we utilized the GeneMANIA (https://genemania.org/) to identify genes with similar functions that interact with these two target genes. The GeneMANIA analysis was performed based on the default settings.

sec.title: Reverse-transcription quantitative polymerase chain reaction (RT-qPCR)
sec.p: Total RNA was extracted from blood samples using Trizol according to the manufacturer’s instruction. Reverse transcription of RNA into cDNA was completed with EasyScript First-Strand cDNA Synthesis SuperMix. RT-qPCR was performed using Green One-Step qRT-PCR SuperMix. 18s served as internal control. Primer sequences for DLGAP5 were as follows: F: AAGTTGTGCAGCCTGTAATG; R: CAGCTCTTGTGACTGGCTTT. Primer sequences for SIRT6 were as follows: F: GTCTTCCAGTGTGGTGTTCC; R: CTCAAAGGTGGTGTCGAACT. The 2−△△Ct method was used for semi-quantitative analysis.

sec.title: Statistical analyses
sec.p: All statistical analyses were performed using R (v4.3.0). The R package “ggplot2” was used for Manhattan plots, and “forestplot” was used for forest plots.To assess the robustness of the findings against multiple testing, we calculated the False Discovery Rate (FDR) using the Benjamini-Hochberg method. While a nominal P_SMR < 0.05 was used as the primary threshold to identify potential associations in this exploratory multi-omics study, FDR values are provided in the Supplementary Tables for reference. The code for plotting SMRLocusPlot and SMREffectPlot was sourced from Pavlides et al. [25].

sec.title: Atherosclerosis GWAS and macrophage polarization-related blood mQTL data
sec.p: Initial SMR analysis identified a substantial number of associations; however, to differentiate vertical pleiotropy from linkage disequilibrium, we applied the HEIDI test. As systematically presented in Supplementary Table S2, we observed that 27.72% (mQTL), 27.17% (eQTL), and 30.30% (pQTL) of the significant SMR signals in the FinnGen cohort failed to pass the HEIDI threshold (P_HEIDI < 0.05) and were excluded due to potential heterogeneity. Ultimately, using the stringent thresholds of P_SMR_multi < 0.05$, P_SMR < 0.05, and P_HEIDI > 0.05, we identified 155 high-confidence methylation sites associated with atherosclerosis, corresponding to 82 genes. Among these identified significant signals, 41 methylation sites, corresponding to 14 genes, had strong colocalization evidence (PPH4 > 0.5). The full analysis content obtained by SMR analysis is shown in Supplementary Table S3.

Figure 2 displays the colocalization results of methylation sites and SNP sites associated with atherosclerosis, 41 methylation sites corresponding to 14 genes were identified in the co-localization region window of the SNP (PPH4 > 0.5). For instance, the methylation level of cg10130446 at the DLGAP5 gene locus is negatively associated with atherosclerosis risk (Figure S1).

caption.p: Forest plot of the mQTLs SMR analysis results of the FinnGen_I9_ATHSCLE cohort

sec.p: The mQTL SMR results were validated for AGPAT4 (cg00692088), CD47 (cg06489037), HNF4A (cg08407434, cg12363404), SMAD3 (cg19193595) methylation sites in the UKB cohort (P_SMR_multi < 0.05 & P_SMR < 0.05 and P-HEIDI > 0.05), and the relationship between methylation level and atherosclerosis risk was consistent with the results of the FinnGen cohort. The full analysis content of the UKB cohort SMR analysis is shown in Supplementary Table S4.

sec.title: Atherosclerosis GWAS and macrophage polarization-related blood eQTL data
sec.p: We identified 14 macrophage polarization-related genes significantly associated with atherosclerosis risk in eQTL analysis, which were shown in Fig. 3 and Supplementary Table S5 (P_SMR_multi < 0.05 & P_SMR < 0.05 and P-HEIDI > 0.05). Among them, high-level expression of 6 genes, for example, DDIT3 (OR = 1.185, 95% CI [1.024–1.372]), DLGAP5 (OR = 1.493, 95% CI [1.065–2.093]), was positively correlated with the risk of atherosclerosis. On the contrary, high-level expression of the remaining genes, for instance, CHD1 (OR = 0.596, 95% CI [0.387–0.917]), DNMT3A (OR = 0.797, 95% CI [0.637–0.997]), was negatively correlated with the risk of atherosclerosis.

caption.p: Forest plot of the eQTLs SMR analysis results of the FinnGen_I9_ATHSCLE cohort

sec.p: The co-localization analysis results showed that there were sites of PRKAB1 and SIRT6 associated with atherosclerosis in the co-localization region window of the SNPs corresponding to the two genes (PPH4 > 0.5) (Figure S2).
The eQTL SMR results were not validated in the UKB cohort (P_SMR_multi < 0.05 & P_SMR < 0.05 and P-HEIDI > 0.05) (Supplementary Table S6).

sec.title: Atherosclerosis GWAS and macrophage polarization-related blood pQTL data
sec.p: The causal relationship between macrophage polarization-related proteins and atherosclerosis was analyzed using SMR. Comprehensive results are provided in Supplementary Table S7. According to the thresholds of P_SMR_multi < 0.05, P_SMR < 0.05, and P-HEIDI > 0.05, four protein, BST2, LMNB1, NINJ1 and TNF were found to be significantly associated with atherosclerosis (Fig. 4A). Among them, BST2 had strong colocalization evidence under the criteria of PPH4 > 0.5. The specific colocalization results of the proteins and atherosclerosis-associated SNPs are depicted in Figure S3. However, the above gene-encoded protein were not validated in the UKB cohort (Supplementary Table S8). Figure 4B shows the distribution of the SMR analysis results of pQTLs in the FinnGen_I9_ATHSCLE cohort across the chromosomes.

caption.p: Results of SMR analysis of pQTLs in the FinnGen_I9_ATHSCLE cohort. A forest plot, B Manhattan plot

sec.title: Integrating evidence from multi-omics levels
sec.p: A comprehensive SMR analysis was performed integrating blood mQTL, eQTL, and pQTL data. The analysis identified five intersecting genes (SIRT6, IL4I1, DNMT3A, DLGAP5, and NINJ1) that may have causal associations with atherosclerosis. We further explored the association between methylation sites and gene expression of key macrophage polarization-related genes in atherosclerosis (mQTL-eQTL) and blood gene expression-regulated key macrophage polarization-related proteins in atherosclerosis (eQTL-pQTL) through SMR analysis. The possible regulatory relationship between mQTL and eQTL related to atherosclerosis is shown in Table 2. Under the criteria of P_SMR_multi < 0.05 & P_SMR < 0.05 and P-HEIDI > 0.05, three methylation sites corresponding to two genes: DLGAP5 (cg10130446) and DNMT3A (cg08485187 and cg17742416), may play crucial role in the development of the atherosclerosis disease (Fig. 5). Specifically, cg10130446 of gene DLGAP5 negatively associated with its gene expression (OR = 0.868, 95% CI [0.833–0.904]). Similarly, the high expression of two methylation sites of gene DNMT3A, cg08485187 (OR = 0.695, 95% CI [0.629–0.769]) and cg17742416 (OR = 0.612, 95% CI [0.516–0.726]), downregulate its gene expression. However, further verification results of eQTL-pQTL showed that there were no positive results in this part of the analysis.

caption.p: Possible regulatory relationships between mQTL and eQTL
Manhattan plots of mQTL (upper) and eQTLs (lower) in FinnGen_I9_ATHSCLE cohort

sec.p: In the mQTL data, the methylation site cg10130446 for DLGAP5 was found to be inversely associated with atherosclerosis risk (OR = 0.938, 95% CI [0.894–0.983]). Conversely, in the eQTL data, DLGAP5 showed a positive association with atherosclerosis risk (OR = 1.493, 95% CI [1.065–2.093]). Furthermore, the mQTL-eQTL analysis indicated a negative regulatory relationship between cg10130446 and DLGAP5 expression (OR = 0.868, 95% CI [0.833–0.904]). Therefore, based on these findings, a hypothetical mechanism can be proposed: higher methylation levels at cg10130446 downregulate the expression of DLGAP5, thereby reducing the risk of atherosclerosis.

For gene DNMT3A, the mQTL analysis identified 7 methylation sites significantly associated with the atherosclerosis risk. Specifically, high level of one methylation site cg15150970 (OR = 1.493, 95% CI [1.065–2.093]) positively regulate the risk of the disease, while the remaining methylation sites negatively positively associated with disease. In the eQTL analysis, DNMT3A showed a negative association with atherosclerosis risk (OR = 0.797, 95% CI [0.637–0.997]). Furthermore, the mQTL-eQTL analysis indicated a negative regulatory relationship between identified two methylation sites, cg08485187 (OR = 0.695, 95% CI [0.629–0.769]) and cg17742416 (OR = 0.612, 95% CI [0.516–0.726]) and DNMT3A expression. There may be a hypothesized mechanism by which higher methylation levels of cg08485187 and cg08485187 down-regulate DNMT3A gene expression, thereby increasing the risk of atherosclerosis.

Figures S4A and S5A illustrate the genetic consistency between atherosclerosis and eQTLs, as well as mQTLs, using locus zoom plots to highlight specific genomic loci. Figure S4B and S5B presents the SMREffectPlot evaluating the potential causal effects of the eQTL and mQTL on atherosclerosis, rather than directly demonstrating genetic consistency.

sec.title: Tissue-specific eQTL validation
sec.p: We further investigated the causal relationship between the expression of identified genes and atherosclerosis in specific tissues using eQTL-GWAS summary-level Mendelian randomization (SMR) analysis in artery aorta, coronary, and tibial tissues. Stringent thresholds were applied, including P_SMR_multi < 0.05, P_SMR < 0.05, and P-HEIDI > 0.05. Notably, the expression of the SIRT6 gene showed a significant association with atherosclerosis risk in both artery aorta and tibial tissues, consistent with the risk direction observed in blood-based eQTL-GWAS findings from the FinnGen cohort. However, no significant association was detected for SIRT6 in coronary artery tissue. Detailed results of the SMR analysis for artery aorta, coronary, and tibial tissues are provided in Supplementary Tables S9–S11.

sec.title: Identification of differential genes associated with atherosclerosis
sec.p: To validate the significance of key signals in atherosclerosis, we acquired a total of 15,315 differentially expressed genes among atherosclerotic and control arteries from GSE100927. The differentially expressed genes were visualized using a heatmap (Fig. 6A) and a volcano plot (Fig. 6B), where blue indicated downregulated genes, while red signified upregulated genes. As seen in Fig. 6C, the atherosclerotic tissues could be clearly distinguished from the control tissues. Furthermore, we found that compared to control tissues, the expression of DLGAP5 and SIRT6 was heightened in atherosclerotic tissues (Fig. 6D-E). More specifically, the relatively higher expression of DLGAP5 and SIRT6 could be validated in atherosclerotic carotid, femoral and infra-popliteal arteries (Fig. 6F-G). This result was consistent with the detrimental role of DLGAP5 from the eQTL results.

caption.p: The elevated expression of DLGAP5 and SIRT6 in atherosclerotic tissues from GSE100927. The differentially expressed genes between control and atheroslcerosis groups were illustrated in a A heatmap and B volcano plot. C Principle component analysis of gene expression profiles from control and atheroslcerosis groups. Barplots depicting the higher expressions of D DLGAP5 and E SIRT6 in atherosclerotic tissues. Barplots depicting the higher expressions of F DLGAP5 and G SIRT6 in carotid, femoral and infra-popliteal atherosclerosis

sec.title: Enrichment analysis of DLGAP5 and SIRT6
sec.p: GO enrichment analysis indicated that these two genes were involved in DNA damage repair, regulation of gene expression and histone deacetylase activity (Figure S6A). KEGG identified that these genes were implicated in nicotinate and nicotinamide metabolism and thermogenesis pathways (Figure S6B).

sec.title: Gene-gene interaction network
sec.p: The interactions between DLGAP5, SIRT6, and genes with similar functions were explored using GeneMANIA. The analysis revealed that DLGAP5 and SIRT6 were associated with 20 functionally similar genes, most of which were other isoforms (Figure S7).

sec.title: Experimental validation
sec.p: To validate the expression of DLGAP5 and SIRT6 in atherosclerosis, we collected blood samples from patients with atherosclerosis and healthy controls and and measured the mRNA levels of these genes. Then we evaluated the mRNA levels of DLGAP5 and SIRT6. The result demonstrated an increase in both DLGAP5 and SIRT6 expressions, which is consistent with the eQTL-GWAS findings (Fig. 7).

caption.p: The elevated expression of DLGAP5 and SIRT6 in blood from patients with atherosclerosis. Barplots demonstrated an increase in both DLGAP5 and SIRT6 in blood samples from atherosclerosis patients (n = 6) compared to healthy controls (n = 6). ** P < 0.01, ***P < 0.005

sec.title: Discussion
sec.p: This study investigated the causal relationships between macrophage polarization-related genetic factors and atherosclerosis using SMR approach. We integrated genetic data from mQTL, eQTL, and pQTL analyses to identify key genes associated with atherosclerosis. Upon integrating the multi-omics data, we identified two genes associated with atherosclerosis risk: DNMT3A and DLGAP5. Additionally, the expression of the SIRT6 gene demonstrated a significant association with atherosclerosis risk in both aortic and tibial artery tissues. Transcriptomic analysis using further confirmed the elevated expression of DLGAP5 and SIRT6 in atherosclerosis patients, supporting their role in disease progression.

Among the key genes identified, DLGAP5 and DNMT3A stood out with robust evidence linking them to atherosclerosis. DLGAP5 is known to function as an oncoprotein, playing significant roles in multiple cancer types by promoting cell proliferation, migration, and invasion [29]. Specifically, in hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC), DLGAP5 exhibits high expression levels compared to normal liver tissues, and its elevated expression correlates with poor clinical outcomes and tumor immune cell infiltration, indicating its potential role in modulating the tumor microenvironment [30]. Furthermore, studies have shown that DLGAP5 promotes gallbladder cancer (GBC) progression and induces macrophage M2 polarization through the activation of the cAMP pathway, enhancing tumor growth and metastasis [31]. In ovarian cancer, the dysregulation of DLGAP5 impact granulosa cell apoptosis and proliferation. Notably, DLGAP5 knockdown suppresses viability and proliferation while enhancing apoptosis and disrupting the cell cycle, which implies its critical role in ovarian cancer pathogenesis [32]. Although direct evidence linking DLGAP5 to macrophage polarization in ovarian cancer is limited, the gene’s impact on cancer development and immune response suggests a possible indirect effect on the tumor-associated macrophages. Collectively, although direct evidence linking DLGAP5 with atherosclerosis is lacking, current findings suggests that DLGAP5 may modulate macrophage polarization and therefore results in various disease. Our study indicated that DLGAP5’s methylation site cg10130446 demonstrated a significant negative association with atherosclerosis risk, suggesting that higher methylation levels at this site reduce DLGAP5 expression, which in turn lowers disease risk. Furthermore, the elevated expression of DLGAP5 was confirmed in atherosclerotic tissues and blood samples. Further research is needed to elucidate the relationship between DLGAP5 and atherosclerosis and clarify the mechanism by which DLGAP5 affects this condition.

DNMT3A, a methyltransferase critical for de novo DNA methylation, has emerged as a key regulator in the pathogenesis of atherosclerosis through its epigenetic modifications that influence gene expression and cellular function. Mutations in DNMT3A associated with clonal hematopoiesis promote a pro-inflammatory state in macrophages, leading to increased activation of inflammatory pathways and accelerated atherosclerotic lesion development, a mechanism comparable to that observed with TET2 mutations [33]. DNMT3A also impacts m6A RNA methylation, a key post-transcriptional regulatory mechanism, which may influence endothelial cell adhesion and smooth muscle cell proliferation, contributing to plaque formation and instability [34]. Additionally, loss-of-function mutations in DNMT3A are linked to altered DNA methylation patterns in macrophages, which promote inflammasome activation and cytokine secretion, amplifying chronic inflammation in atherosclerotic plaques [35]. Furthermore, DNMT3A deficiency leads to several potentially pro-atherogenic phenotypes in various immune cell populations, including pro-inflammatory activation of mast cells [36], increased IFNγ production by T cells, and reduced immunosuppressive function in myeloid-derived suppressor cells. Conversely, DNMT3A inhibition has been shown to increase IL-13 expression in T cells and limit type I interferon production in macrophages, which could protect against atherosclerosis development [37, 38]. Together, these findings suggest that DNMT3A acts as a crucial mediator of epigenetic regulation in atherosclerosis, and are consistent with our study results. The negative regulatory relationship between methylation at cg08485187 and cg17742416 and DNMT3A expression suggests that epigenetic dysregulation may contribute to increased disease risk, underscoring the need for targeted investigations into macrophage polarization-mediated pathways.

SIRT6, validated across blood and arterial tissues, is known for regulating inflammation and metabolism, both critical in atherosclerosis. Previous studies have shown that SIRT6 modulates inflammatory responses in macrophages, reinforcing its involvement in atherosclerosis. SIRT6, a member of the sirtuin family of NAD-dependent deacetylases, has been shown to play a crucial role in various cardiovascular pathologies [39, 40]. SIRT6 is unique due to its chromatin-associated deacetylase activity, which imparts several protective effects similar to those of SIRT1 [41–43]. These include inhibition of heart failure and slowing down the aging process in mice [44, 45]. SIRT6 is also involved in reducing endothelial inflammation and aging, as well as in regulating dendritic cell differentiation, maturation, and function. Decreased SIRT6 expression has been observed in endothelial cells under chronic conditions such as exposure to lipopolysaccharide (LPS) [45], hydrogen peroxide (H2O2) [46], and high glucose [47–49], which are known risk factors for endothelial dysfunction and atherogenesis. Studies have further reported reduced SIRT6 levels in atherosclerotic models such as ApoE−/− mice and human patients [50, 51]. Additionally, genetic variants of SIRT6 have been linked to the severity of coronary artery disease (CAD) [52]. Consistently, our findings revealed an increased expression of SIRT6 in atherosclerotic tissues and blood, highlighting the relevance of SIRT6 in the disease pathology. These findings suggest that SIRT6 represents a promising candidate for future functional studies to elucidate its specific role in macrophage polarization and atherosclerosis progression.

In this study, we employed SMR analysis to investigate the causal relationship between macrophage polarization-related genes and atherosclerosis. Utilizing a multi-omics strategy—encompassing methylation, gene expression, and protein levels—we aimed to construct a regulatory network that elucidates the synergistic roles of macrophage polarization-related genes in atherosclerosis progression. Integrating data across multiple omics layers allowed us to systematically explore and enhance the reliability and depth of our insights into this pathology, followed by tissue-level validation and transcriptome-based confirmation of key signals in atherosclerotic tissues. While our study employs a multi-omics approach to investigate the relationship between macrophage polarization-related genes and atherosclerosis, several limitations must be considered. Firstly, the study’s observational nature restricts our ability to definitively establish causality. Secondly, the key genes identified in blood eQTL analyses were not validated by tissue-specific studies, underscoring the need for future research to bridge this gap. Importantly, our analysis relies heavily on aggregate-level data from populations predominantly of European ancestry, which may limit the generalizability of our findings to other ethnic groups. Additionally, the pQTL dataset utilized in this study relies on plasma samples; the current scarcity of large-scale pQTL data derived specifically from atherosclerotic tissues or macrophages limits the resolution of tissue-specific protein-level associations. Furthermore, we acknowledge the inherent limitations of the HEIDI test in distinguishing pleiotropy from causality. While a $P_{HEIDI} > 0.05$ threshold is standard for filtering out heterogeneity, this test may have limited statistical power, particularly in regions with complex LD structures or when the number of instrumental SNPs is small. Therefore, although we applied rigorous filtering and excluded approximately 27–30% of potential artifacts (Supplementary Table S2), we cannot entirely rule out the possibility that some identified associations might be influenced by residual linkage disequilibrium. Finally, the lack of in-depth experimental validation in biological models represents a limitation of the current study. To address this, our future investigations will focus on elucidating the specific molecular mechanisms using gene-knockout or overexpression techniques in both macrophage cell lines and atherosclerotic murine models. Concurrently, we plan to expand our clinical cohort collection to verify these findings in a larger and more diverse population, thereby further establishing the clinical relevance and robustness of the prioritized candidate genes.

sec.title: Conclusions
sec.p: In conclusion, this study explored the potential role of macrophage polarization-related genes in atherosclerosis through SMR combined with multi-omics analysis, and discussed the possible mechanism of three crucial genes, DLGAP5, DNMT3A and SIRT6 associated with the disease. These findings not only highlight the complex role of epigenetic regulation in disease progression, but also suggest that future studies should aim to uncover the complex interactions between these genes, aiming to fully elucidate the pathophysiological mechanisms by which macrophage polarization and atherosclerosis are intertwined. This might potentially provide a theoretical basis for understanding the genetic architecture of the disease and prioritizing candidate genes for future experimental validation.
